lead: A vector space gives you exactly two moves: scale a vector, and add two vectors. A linear combination is one round of both — multiply each vector by a number, then add. Gather every vector you can build this way from a set S and you have the span of S, the smallest subspace that holds S. Spans turn a short list of vectors into a whole line, plane or space, so they describe solution sets, the reachable states of a control system, and every column of a matrix at once.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.1 for the ten vector space rules and Chapter 2.2 for the subspace test, plus Unit 1 for solving linear systems by elimination.

blocks.text: Take vectors v₁, v₂, …, vₖ from a vector space V over a field F, and scalars c₁, c₂, …, cₖ from F. The single vector c₁v₁ + c₂v₂ + ⋯ + cₖvₖ is a linear combination of v₁, …, vₖ. The scalars cᵢ are its coefficients.

blocks.where: vᵢ are vectors in V; cᵢ are scalars (coefficients) from the field F, which is R or C here; k ≥ 1 is a finite count.

blocks.text: Only two operations appear: scalar multiplication and addition. There are no powers, no products of two vectors, and no constant term added at the end. That is why the combination is called linear.

In R³ take v₁ = (1, 2, 0) and v₂ = (0, 1, 1). Then 3v₁ − v₂ = (3, 6, 0) − (0, 1, 1) = (3, 5, −1) is a linear combination with c₁ = 3 and c₂ = −1. The choice c₁ = c₂ = 0 gives the zero vector (0, 0, 0).
Every combination uses finitely many vectors. Addition and scaling act on two or three vectors at a time; the definition has no infinite sum in it.

sections.h3: The span of a set is a subspace

blocks.text: For a set S ⊆ V, the span of S, written span(S), is the set of all linear combinations of finitely many vectors of S.
span(S) = { c₁v₁ + ⋯ + cₖvₖ : k ≥ 0, vᵢ ∈ S, cᵢ ∈ F }
blocks.where: k = 0 is allowed and gives the empty sum, which is the zero vector; the vectors vᵢ are picked from S and may repeat.

blocks.text: Two conventions follow. span(∅) = {0}, because the only combination you can form is the empty one. And 0 always lies in span(S), by setting every cᵢ = 0.

items: 0 = 0·v₁ + ⋯ + 0·vₖ, so the zero vector is in span(S).
If u = Σaᵢvᵢ and w = Σbⱼwⱼ are in span(S), then u + w = Σaᵢvᵢ + Σbⱼwⱼ is again a finite combination of vectors of S.
If c ∈ F, then cu = Σ(caᵢ)vᵢ is in span(S), since each caᵢ is still a scalar.
These three facts are exactly the subspace test of Chapter 2.2, so span(S) is a subspace of V.

blocks.text: It is also the smallest subspace containing S. Let W be any subspace with S ⊆ W. A subspace is closed under scaling and addition, so W already holds every combination of vectors of S; hence span(S) ⊆ W. Therefore span(S) sits inside every subspace that contains S, and the span is their intersection: span(S) = ⋂ {W : W is a subspace of V and S ⊆ W}.

sections.h3: Membership test, pictures and spanning sets

blocks.text: Membership test. Given v₁, …, vₖ in Fⁿ and a target b, ask whether b = c₁v₁ + ⋯ + cₖvₖ has a solution. Put the vᵢ as the columns of A = [v₁ ⋯ vₖ] and let x = (c₁, …, cₖ)ᵗ. Then b lies in span{v₁, …, vₖ} exactly when Ax = b is consistent, which happens exactly when rank(A) = rank([A | b]). Test it by Gaussian elimination, as in Unit 1.

Pictures. One non-zero vector v in R³ spans the line {cv : c ∈ R} through the origin. Two vectors that are not multiples of each other span a plane through the origin. A single vector, or the zero vector alone, gives only that line or only the origin — the count of vectors never settles the shape on its own.

Spanning sets. When span(S) = V we say S spans V, and S is a spanning set of V. Some syllabi write generating set, linear hull, or closed linear span for the same object. Adding vectors to S can only enlarge the span. Removing a vector that already lies in the span of the others leaves the span unchanged, so a spanning set can be trimmed without losing reach; that trimming idea becomes the basis in Chapter 2.5.

spec.title: Span of two vectors in R³
spec.aria: Two vectors combine by scaling and adding into a whole plane through the origin, and the single point (2,5,1) is one such combination.

examples.question: In R³ let v₁ = (1, 2, 0) and v₂ = (0, 1, 1). Is the vector (2, 5, 1) in span{v₁, v₂}? If yes, give the coefficients.
steps: We need scalars a, b with a(1, 2, 0) + b(0, 1, 1) = (2, 5, 1). Reading coordinates separately gives three scalar equations.
First coordinate: a·1 + b·0 = 2, so a = 2.
Third coordinate: a·0 + b·1 = 1, so b = 1.
Second coordinate must then read 2a + b = 2(2) + 1 = 5. The target's second coordinate is 5, so the equation holds and the system is consistent.
examples.answer: Yes, (2, 5, 1) lies in span{v₁, v₂}, namely (2, 5, 1) = 2v₁ + 1v₂, with coefficients a = 2 and b = 1.
examples.check:
v1 = (1, 2, 0)
v2 = (0, 1, 1)
target = (2, 5, 1)

a = target[0] // v1[0]        # first coordinate: a*1 + b*0 = 2
b = target[2] // v2[2]        # third coordinate:  a*0 + b*1 = 1
second = a * v1[1] + b * v2[1]  # predicted second coordinate

print(a)
print(b)
print(second)

traps: Writing the target vector as a row when the given vectors are columns. The system changes shape and so does the answer; keep the vᵢ as columns of A and b on the right.
Assuming more vectors means a bigger span. In R³ three vectors that are all multiples of one vector span only a line, and two vectors with one a multiple of the other span only a line too.
Confusing S with span(S). The span is usually far larger than S, and it always contains 0 even when S does not.
Treating span(A) ∪ span(B) as a subspace. It is usually not one; the honest statement is span(A ∪ B) = span(A) + span(B), the sum of subspaces from Chapter 2.2.
Stopping after two coordinates. The remaining equations are the test: a = 2 and b = 1 must also satisfy the second coordinate, and an examiner will ask for that check.

quiz.q: Define a linear combination of vectors v₁, …, vₖ, and name its coefficients.
quiz.a: For scalars c₁, …, cₖ in the field F, the vector c₁v₁ + ⋯ + cₖvₖ is a linear combination of v₁, …, vₖ; the scalars cᵢ are the coefficients.
span(∅) = {0}, because the only combination of vectors of the empty set is the empty sum, which equals the zero vector.

quiz.q: Why is span(S) a subspace of V?
quiz.a: The zero vector is 0·v₁ + ⋯ + 0·vₖ, so it is in span(S). Adding two combinations gives another combination of vectors of S, and multiplying a combination by a scalar multiplies each coefficient. The three subspace test conditions hold.

quiz.q: In what sense is span(S) the smallest subspace containing S?
quiz.a: Any subspace W containing S is closed under scaling and addition, so it already contains every combination of vectors of S. Hence span(S) ⊆ W for every such W, and span(S) equals the intersection of all subspaces containing S.

quiz.q: With v₁ = (1, 2, 0) and v₂ = (0, 1, 1), is (1, 1, 1) in span{v₁, v₂}?
quiz.a: Solve a(1,2,0) + b(0,1,1) = (1,1,1). First coordinate a = 1, third coordinate b = 1. Second coordinate then reads 2(1) + 1 = 3, but the target has 1. Inconsistent, so (1, 1, 1) is not in the span.

quiz.q: With v₁ = (1, 2, 0) and v₂ = (0, 1, 1), is (3, 5, −1) in span{v₁, v₂}? Give the coefficients.
quiz.a: First coordinate a = 3, third coordinate b = −1. Second coordinate: 2(3) + (−1) = 5, which matches. So (3, 5, −1) = 3v₁ − v₂ is in the span.

quiz.q: Let S = {(1,0,0), (0,1,0), (1,1,0)} in R³. Show that span(S) equals the span of the first two vectors, and describe the subspace.
quiz.a: The third vector is the sum of the first two, so it is already in their span and adds nothing. span(S) = {a(1,0,0) + b(0,1,0)} = {(a, b, 0) : a, b ∈ R}, the xy-plane, a subspace of dimension 2.

quiz.q: True or false: if v₃ ∈ span{v₁, v₂}, then span{v₁, v₂, v₃} = span{v₁, v₂}. Justify.
quiz.a: True. Write v₃ = αv₁ + βv₂. Any c₁v₁ + c₂v₂ + c₃v₃ becomes (c₁ + c₃α)v₁ + (c₂ + c₃β)v₂, a combination of v₁ and v₂. The reverse inclusion is immediate since both v₁, v₂ are in span{v₁, v₂, v₃}.

beyond: Not for the exam. In control engineering the set of states a system can reach from rest is exactly a span of the input directions pushed through the dynamics, and checking reachability is a rank test on that spanning set. In machine learning the predictions of a linear model live in the span of the feature columns, which is why redundant features change nothing about what the model can fit. Over the two-element field, linear error-correcting codes are spans of a few generator words. Search next for column space, reachable subspace, and generator matrix.
